subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage: Dolma, sit down. I'm your uncle Tanvir, and I was twenty-four when a clerk at the ward office sent me from counter to counter for a copy of my birth certificate. At the third counter he said, without looking up, "Files move faster with a little tea money." My face went hot. I wanted to shout, and part of me wanted to just pay. Instead I kept my voice level and said, "Could you please show me the fee and the rule in writing?" He shrugged. I thanked him, noted his counter number and the date, and walked to the notice board where the grievance officer's name and helpline were printed. I filed a written complaint that afternoon and got a receipt number. Ten days later I had the certificate, no tea money paid, and a clerk who avoided my eyes.

qa.q: What did the clerk say at the third counter?
qa.a: He said files move faster with a little tea money.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when the clerk hinted at tea money?
qa.a: Angry and torn: Tanvir's face went hot, wanting to shout and also to just pay.

qa.q: What choices at the counter kept Tanvir safe and effective?
qa.a: Tanvir stayed polite, asked for the fee and rule in writing, noted the counter number and date, and filed a written complaint.

qa.q: How might the clerk have felt when Tanvir calmly asked for the rule in writing?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable and caught out, since the clerk only shrugged and later avoided Tanvir's eyes.

grounding: Shows a citizen hinted toward an extra payment who stays polite, asks for the rule in writing and uses the official complaint route.

subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage: The office shut at four, and Ishita's job offer needed stamped address proof by morning. At half past two the clerk pointed her to window six, window six pointed back, and then a man in the corner leaned close. "Two hundred and it's done today." Her hands shook. Outside, her brother Sachin muttered, "Just pay it." Ishita took a breath. "Not today. I'll ask for the rule." At the window she said, "Could you write the fee and the steps on my form, please?" The officer on duty looked up, wrote both, and stamped it himself. Ishita also asked at the desk where complaints go and copied the number into her phone. She reached the car park with ten minutes to spare.

qa.q: What amount did the man in the corner ask for?
qa.a: He asked for two hundred to get it done today.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when the man in the corner leaned close?
qa.a: Shaken and angry, since her hands shook and she refused to simply pay.

qa.q: What did Ishita do instead of paying, and what did it achieve?
qa.a: She politely asked for the fee and steps in writing, and the officer wrote both and stamped the form; she also copied the complaint number.

qa.q: Why might Sachin have said "Just pay it"?
qa.a: Sachin was probably anxious about the four o'clock deadline and wanted the fastest way out for his sister.

grounding: Shows a citizen sent from window to window and hinted toward paying extra, who stays polite, asks for the rule in writing and notes the complaint route.

subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage:
Kamal, you asked why I looked so tired last month. Let me, Francis, tell you the whole electricity story.
After Appa passed, I went to move the connection into my name. Counter A sent me to counter C. Counter C said a form was missing and sent me back to A. Third day, a man outside the building leaned in: "Give a little extra, it'll be done by evening." And the clerk at C said, "You can go through him, it's faster."
I was so angry my hands were shaking. I wanted to shout. I also, honestly, wanted to just pay and be done.
I did neither. I asked the clerk, politely, "Please write down which rule needs this form." He hesitated. Then I asked where the complaint register was. It was right there, on the side table. Suddenly the form wasn't missing anymore. The next week I filed the online grievance anyway, so the next person gets the list on day one.

qa.q: What did the man outside the building say?
qa.a: He said, "Give a little extra, it'll be done by evening."

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when the clerk pointed to the man outside?
qa.a: Francis felt angry, with his hands shaking, and also tempted to just pay and be done with it.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Francis, and why?
qa.a: Staying polite while asking for the rule in writing and for the complaint register worked, because it made the delay hard to keep up without a fight or a bribe.

qa.q: How might the clerk have felt when Francis asked for the complaint register?
qa.a: The clerk was probably uneasy and caught out, since he hesitated and then the missing form was suddenly not missing.

grounding: Illustrates a citizen sent between counters and nudged toward an extra payment who stays polite, asks for the rule in writing and uses the complaint route.

subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage:
Day one, a Monday. Rashmi reached the ration office at ten to add her new baby's name to the family card. Counter two sent her to counter five. Counter five said the officer was "on leave, come Thursday." Rashmi went home with the baby asleep on her shoulder and her jaw tight.
Thursday. The officer was in, but a man by the gate offered to "fast-track" it for an amount he whispered. Tenzin, her neighbour who had come along, raised his eyebrows. Rashmi felt her face burn. She walked away without answering.
The following Monday she came back with Tenzin and a notebook. At the counter she asked calmly, "Please write down which documents are needed and how many days it takes." The officer wrote it on the back of a form and signed it. Rashmi also noted the complaint number on the wall. Ten days later, the new card came.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi go to the ration office?
qa.a: She went to add her new baby's name to the family card.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when the man at the gate made his offer?
qa.a: Rashmi felt insulted and angry; her face burned, and she walked away without answering.

qa.q: What made the third visit work?
qa.a: Asking calmly for the documents and the timeline in writing, getting it signed and noting the complaint number, instead of arguing or paying.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see the man's offer?
qa.a: Tenzin seems uneasy and disapproving, raising his eyebrows, and he supports Rashmi by coming back with her.

grounding: Shows a citizen sent from counter to counter and hinted toward an extra payment who calmly asks for the rule in writing and knows the complaint route.

subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage:
Anjali, sit. Your Damini maasi will tell you about my first pension claim, the year after your nana retired.
I was twenty-five. The clerk at the district office kept my file under a stack of others for six weeks. Each time I went, he said, "Some paper is missing." Never which paper. Once he rubbed his thumb and finger together and smiled. I went home and cried in the bathroom, so angry I could not eat.
My friend Beena said, "Don't shout, and don't pay. Ask him to write down the rule." So next time I stood at his window and said, very politely, "Sir, kindly write which paper is missing and under which order." He stopped smiling. Then I asked where the grievance box was. The file moved in four days.
I was shaking the whole time, Anjali. Polite is not the same as weak.

qa.q: How long did the clerk keep the file under a stack of others?
qa.a: He kept it under a stack of others for six weeks.

qa.q: What was young Damini feeling after the clerk's gesture?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious, crying in the bathroom and too angry to eat.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking politely for the missing paper and order in writing, and for the grievance box, worked because it made the clerk accountable without a fight or a payment.

qa.q: How might Beena have felt watching her friend struggle?
qa.a: Beena was probably concerned and protective, giving calm, practical advice so Damini would not either shout or pay.

grounding: An elder recalls being stalled and hinted toward a bribe by a clerk and staying polite while asking for the rule in writing and the complaint route.

subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage: Rain came down in sheets, the ward office closed at five, and Sangeeta's mother waited outside in an auto, meter running. Sangeeta only needed her mother's name added to the property tax record. Counter three sent her to counter seven. Counter seven sent her back to three. Darshan, a man in a cream shirt, leaned on a pillar. "Madam, I can finish it today. Give me a little something for the babu, he'll sign." Her ears went hot. She wanted to shout, or just pay. Instead she said, "No, thank you," and went back to counter three. "Sir, could you write down which document is missing and the rule that asks for it? Then I'll bring it." The clerk looked up, surprised. Behind him hung a Citizen's Charter board listing time limits and a ground-floor complaint counter. She glanced at it, still polite. He pulled her file over, stamped two pages and said, "Come Friday for the copy."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta need added to the property tax record?
qa.a: Her mother's name.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when Darshan made his offer?
qa.a: She felt angry and helpless, her ears hot, tempted both to shout and to just pay.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta's request to the clerk work better than arguing or paying?
qa.a: Asking politely for the missing document and the rule in writing, with the complaint counter on the wall, made it hard to keep sending her round without a reason.

qa.q: How might the clerk have seen Sangeeta's written request?
qa.a: The clerk seemed caught off guard, perhaps realising she knew her rights and would not pay or give up, and chose to process the file.

grounding: Shows a citizen sent between counters and nudged towards a bribe who stays polite, asks for the rule in writing and points to the complaint route.
